hypothesis.title: The Thick Boundary
hypothesis.question: What changes when composers treat musical boundaries as zones with measurable width rather than point events?
hypothesis.hypothesis: Musical transitions become more intelligible and expressive when their boundaries are composed as thick regions of overlap, uncertainty, handoff, or relational crossing rather than as instantaneous cuts.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: Forced-alignment research models phoneme transitions as confidence intervals, suggesting that sound-category changes naturally occupy regions rather than instants. Bioacoustic work adds two complementary boundary cases: millisecond annotation for sparse animal calls, and multi-band encoding where spectral cutoffs define which acoustic worlds remain visible to a model or listener. Tonnetz geometry treats harmonic adjacency itself as a boundary rule determined by the chosen graph. Video-to-music generation exposes the seam between high-level semantic planning and rendered sound, while call-and-response production practice shows that the gap or overlap between gestures carries musical grammar. Together these sources suggest a composition method centered on boundary thickness.

recipe.title: Boundary Thickness Study
recipe.bodyMd: Create a one-minute sketch with three explicit boundary types: temporal, spectral, and relational. For the temporal boundary, morph one vocal or instrumental gesture over a measured window rather than cutting at the gridline. For the spectral boundary, split a sound into bands and let only some bands answer or anticipate the next gesture. For the relational boundary, define harmonic movement by a graph adjacency rule and include one deliberate long-distance crossing. Render a thin-boundary version and a thick-boundary version using the same source material, then compare which one makes transition, anticipation, and response more audible.
dawChecklist: Choose one short call-response phrase and duplicate it into thin/thick versions.
Set temporal boundary widths explicitly, e.g. 0 ms, 80 ms, 180 ms, and 350 ms.
Split one layer into low/mid/high bands and stagger their entries independently.
Choose a harmonic adjacency rule, then mark one intentional long graph-distance jump.
A/B test whether listeners describe the thick version as morphing, anticipating, breathing, or blurring.

protocol.listeningContext: Nearfield monitors or headphones at moderate level
protocol.listeningMethod: Blind A/B between thin-boundary and thick-boundary renders
